A multi-language tutorial relating EEG/ERP measures to neuropsychological performance — worked case studies, real results, code in Python, R, and Matlab.

Start the tutorial See the case studies

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This tutorial provides two complete, worked case studies on a common clinical research question: how do EEG/ERP measures relate to neuropsychological performance? Each one follows a full pipeline — data wrangling, descriptive statistics, association analysis, modelling and diagnostics, export — with plain-language explanations aimed at readers with no statistics background.

Case Study 1 · Python & R ERP correlates of neuropsychological performance

Two well-characterised ERP components (N400, P300), reduced to four scalar features and related to neuropsychological scores via linear regression — hypothesis-driven, complete and ready-to-run.

Explore the case study → Case Study 2 · Python Whole-scalp spectral analysis of resting-state EEG

Real, whole-scalp EEG spectra analysed with cluster-based permutation testing — no a priori restriction to a single band or region, exploratory by design.

Explore the case study →

docs.title: Case Study 1 · ERP correlates of neuropsychological performance
docs.text:
A hypothesis-driven look at whether two classic ERP components — N400 and P300 — relate to neuropsychological performance in post-stroke patients, using four scalar features and linear regression.

See the code

4 ERP features Linear regression Synthetic data

docs.title: Research question
docs.text:
Are the amplitude and latency of specific ERP components associated with neuropsychological performance and demographic characteristics in post-stroke patients?

This is a hypothesis-driven question: rather than exploring the full spectral or spatiotemporal structure of the EEG signal (see Case Study 2), it targets two specific, well-characterised ERP components:

  • N400 — a negative deflection ~400 ms post-stimulus, indexing semantic processing and language comprehension (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011)
  • P300 — a positive deflection ~300 ms post-target, indexing attentional resource allocation (Polich, 2007)

For each component we consider amplitude (mean µV in a predefined window) and latency (ms of peak amplitude) — four participant-level neural predictors in total.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
The code uses a synthetic (mock) dataset of 40 simulated post-stroke patients, so it can be run end to end without access to real clinical data:

  • dataset_NPSY.csv — demographics (age, sex) and neuropsychological scores (CRIq, APACS, Attentive Matrices, MoCA)
  • dataset_ERP.csv — the four ERP features (N400/P300 amplitude and latency), linked by subject_id

docs.title: A taste of the results
docs.text:
• Pearson correlations between all ERP and neuropsychological variables, annotated with significance stars.

  • The two hypothesised associations (P300 amplitude ↔ Attentive Matrices; N400 latency ↔ APACS), with regression line and 95% CI band.

Key takeaway

More predictors do not make a better model — and how you decide which ones to drop matters as much as the decision itself. Choosing predictors a priori, from theory, avoids the circular reasoning of dropping whatever happens to be non-significant in a bigger model. See the full reasoning in the code, Section 2.3.

See the code

docs.title: Strengths and limitations
docs.text:
Strengths — reduces high-dimensional EEG to four interpretable scalar features; uses regression models that are familiar to clinical researchers; N400 and P300 rest on decades of validation in neurological populations.

Limitations — the predefined time windows and electrode sets may miss effects that are delayed, spatially atypical, or otherwise deviate from the normative pattern the features were designed to capture — a particular risk in a clinical population such as stroke patients. When the question is broader or more exploratory, see Case Study 2.

docs.title: Case Study 2 · Whole-scalp spectral analysis of resting-state EEG
docs.text:
An exploratory, whole-scalp look at resting-state EEG spectra and global cognition — no a priori restriction to a single frequency band or region, analysed with cluster-based permutation testing.

See the code

204 channels × 159 freqs Cluster permutation Real EEG spectra

docs.title: Research question
docs.text:
Does the spectral profile of resting-state EEG relate to global cognitive functioning, without restricting the analysis in advance to a specific frequency band or region?

Where Case Study 1 reduces the EEG signal to four theory-driven scalar features, this case study keeps the full power spectral density (PSD, 1–40 Hz, every channel) and asks broadly where — across the whole scalp and spectrum — resting EEG power relates to global cognition (MoCA). It is motivated by a well-established clinical observation: right-hemisphere stroke is frequently accompanied by pathological EEG slowing (more delta/theta power over the affected region) that tracks the severity of impairment (Finnigan & Van Putten, 2013).

docs.title: Data — and an important disclosure
docs.text:
• The EEG spectra are real, anonymised recordings from the PATHS study (Welch's method, 1–40 Hz), authorised for publication here.
  • The neuropsychological table (age, sex, CRIq, MoCA) is synthetic, as in Case Study 1.
  • Because the two do not come from the same assessment, the moca column was deliberately linked to a real, montage-based property of each EEG recording (see data/generate_datasets.ipynb for the full, explicit disclosure). The resulting brain–behaviour association should not be read as a real clinical finding — it exists so this case study has a real spectrum to analyse and something genuine to recover.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
1. Data Wrangling
  • Strictly align PSD array with neuropsychological table
  • Spectrum data-quality checks
  • Log-power distribution check
2. Analysis
  • Baseline model (Case-Study-1-style, for contrast)
  • Mass-univariate partial correlation
  • Cluster-based permutation (primary + secondary)
  • Exploratory per-band breakdown
3. Export
  • Figures (PNG)
  • Tables (CSV + Excel)

docs.title: A taste of the results
docs.text:
• The real grand-average EEG spectrum: a 1/f-like decay with a visible alpha bump — a first sanity check that the recordings look like EEG.

  • Where the significant effect is: a right-lateralised, low-frequency cluster (marked channels), shown against real data on both hemispheres.

Key takeaway

The primary, whole-spectrum test does not survive correction at n=40 — an honest illustration of the paper's own caveat that cluster-based permutation is relatively underpowered at this sample size. A secondary, pre-registered test restricted to the hypothesised region (right hemisphere, delta/theta) does recover a significant cluster. Reporting both, rather than only the one that "worked", is what keeps the secondary result meaningful — the same a-priori-vs-post-hoc logic Case Study 1 teaches for choosing predictors, applied here to choosing where to look. An exploratory breakdown by individual frequency band (Section 2.7 of the code) makes the trade-off concrete: none of the five canonical bands survives correction on its own, which is exactly why the secondary test pools delta and theta together.

See the code

Exported results, ready to open in Excel or re-use elsewhere:

  • All tables — one workbook, one sheet each
  • Descriptive statistics (CSV)
  • Cluster results — primary & secondary (CSV)
  • Baseline model (CSV)
  • Per-band breakdown, exploratory (CSV)

The code and raw data also live in the GitHub repository, under python/CaseStudy_2/, r/case2/, and data/.

docs.title: Strengths and limitations
docs.text:
Strengths — no a priori commitment to a specific band or region, able to recover a distributed, low-frequency, right-hemisphere pattern that no single ERP feature (Case Study 1) would capture; respects the real spatial and spectral dependency structure of the signal.

Limitations — computationally heavier than the GLM-based approach of Case Study 1; statistically demanding, since cluster-based permutation is relatively underpowered at a sample size like this one, so only fairly marked associations are likely to survive; a significant secondary result is only meaningful because the restricted region was pre-registered before looking at the data — restricting only after seeing what "worked" would be the same circular reasoning Case Study 1 warns against, just at the level of search space instead of predictor selection.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
Matlab has no notebook format, so this is the plain script shown directly (same code, data, and models as the Python/R notebooks). Run it with matlab -batch "run('CaseStudy_1.m')", or open it in the MATLAB editor, from inside matlab/case1/code/ — see the repository README for requirements (MATLAB R2020a+ and the Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox).

% Case Study 1 - Analytical strategy based on reduced EEG features (MATLAB)
%
% This is the MATLAB implementation of Case Study 1 - same data, same
% models, same explanations as the Python and R versions. It implements
% the analysis described in Section 4.1 of the companion paper. Written
% using MATLAB's own table/model classes (readtable, fitlm, histogram,
% exportgraphics) rather than hand-rolled equivalents - see
% matlab/README_matlab.md for requirements.
%
% The research question is:
%   Are the amplitude and latency of specific ERP components associated
%   with neuropsychological performance and demographic characteristics
%   in post-stroke patients?
%
% Two well-characterised ERP components are used:
%   - N400 - a negative deflection ~400 ms post-stimulus, indexing
%     semantic processing (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011)
%   - P300 - a positive deflection ~300 ms post-target, indexing
%     attentional resource allocation (Polich, 2007)
%
% From each component we consider amplitude (mean uV within a predefined
% time window) and latency (ms of peak amplitude), yielding four
% participant-level neural predictors.
%
% Pipeline:
%   1. Data Wrangling  - load, inspect, check ranges, missing data,
%      distributions, outliers
%   2. Analysis        - descriptive stats, bivariate correlations,
%      three regression models, post-hoc assumption checking
%   3. Export          - save tables and figures
%
% All code is defined directly here for transparency and reproducibility.

%% 0. Setup

set(0, "DefaultFigureVisible", "off");  % headless: save figures, never pop up windows

%% Input/output folders

DATA_DIR = fullfile("..", "..", "..", "data");
NPSY_CSV = fullfile(DATA_DIR, "dataset_NPSY.csv");
EEG_CSV  = fullfile(DATA_DIR, "dataset_ERP.csv");

OUTPUTS = fullfile("..", "outputs");
FIGS    = fullfile(OUTPUTS, "figures");
RESULTS = fullfile(OUTPUTS, "results");
if ~exist(FIGS, "dir");    mkdir(FIGS);    end
if ~exist(RESULTS, "dir"); mkdir(RESULTS); end

%% 1. Data Wrangling
%% 1.1 Load data
% The datasets are stored as separate CSV files linked by subject_id.

npsy = readtable(NPSY_CSV);
eeg  = readtable(EEG_CSV);
fprintf("NPSY: %d x %d\n", height(npsy), width(npsy));
fprintf("EEG:  %d x %d\n", height(eeg), width(eeg));

% Both files are generated together and already row-aligned by
% subject_id (see data/generate_datasets.ipynb); we still verify this
% explicitly rather than assuming it, same as the Python/R versions.
assert(isequal(npsy.subject_id, eeg.subject_id), ...
       "NPSY and EEG tables must be row-aligned by subject_id");

df = [npsy, eeg(:, {'n400_amp', 'n400_lat', 'p300_amp', 'p300_lat'})];
n_subj = height(df);
fprintf("Merged: %d subjects x %d variables\n", n_subj, width(df) - 1);

%% 1.2 Initial inspection
% Expected clinical ranges: age 18-100y, CRIq 70-130, N400 amp 1-6uV,
% N400 lat 350-500ms, P300 amp 5-20uV, P300 lat 300-500ms, APACS 0-1,
% Attentive Matrices 0-60, MoCA 0-30.

range_vars = {"age", "criq", "n400_amp", "n400_lat", "p300_amp", "p300_lat", "apacs", "att_matr", "moca"};
range_lo   = [18,     70,     0.5,        300,        3,          250,        0,       0,          0];
range_hi   = [100,    130,    8,          550,        25,         550,        1,       60,         30];

fprintf("Range checks:\n");
any_warn = false;
for i = 1:numel(range_vars)
  col = range_vars{i};
  v = df.(col);
  below = sum(v < range_lo(i));
  above = sum(v > range_hi(i));
  if below > 0
    fprintf("  ! %s: %d values below %g\n", col, below, range_lo(i)); any_warn = true;
  end
  if above > 0
    fprintf("  ! %s: %d values above %g\n", col, above, range_hi(i)); any_warn = true;
  end
end
if ~any_warn
  fprintf("  All values within expected ranges.\n");
end

%% 1.3 Missing data
% Missing data are common in clinical neuropsychological datasets - they
% can arise from fatigue, incomplete testing, or participant dropout.
% Listwise deletion is simple but reduces sample size and may bias
% estimates if data are not missing completely at random (MCAR);
% multiple imputation preserves sample size and is valid under the
% weaker missing-at-random (MAR) assumption, and is generally preferred
% in clinical samples. Our synthetic dataset has complete data for all
% 40 participants, so no imputation is needed here.

vars = {'age', 'sex', 'criq', 'apacs', 'att_matr', 'moca', ...
        'n400_amp', 'n400_lat', 'p300_amp', 'p300_lat'};

miss_mat = ismissing(df(:, vars));
total_missing = sum(miss_mat, "all");

fig_missing = figure("Position", [0 0 900 250]);
if total_missing == 0
  text(0.5, 0.5, "No missing data", "HorizontalAlignment", "center", "FontSize", 14);
  axis off;
else
  imagesc(miss_mat'); colormap(gca, [0.85 0.85 0.85; 0.2 0.2 0.6]);
  set(gca, "YTick", 1:numel(vars), "YTickLabel", vars, "TickLabelInterpreter", "none");
end
title("Missing data matrix");

fprintf("%-25s %8s %8s\n", "Variable", "Missing", "Rate");
fprintf("%s\n", repmat('-', 1, 43));
for i = 1:numel(vars)
  n_miss = sum(miss_mat(:, i));
  fprintf("%-25s %8d %7.1f%%\n", vars{i}, n_miss, n_miss / n_subj * 100);
end

% What do we see in the plot?
%   Each row is a participant, each column a variable; a highlighted
%   cell would mark a missing value. Here the matrix is empty and the
%   per-column rates above all read 0% - this synthetic dataset has no
%   missing data by construction, so there's nothing to impute or
%   exclude. In a real dataset, scattered missingness would support
%   listwise deletion; missingness concentrated in specific participants
%   or variables would be a reason to consider imputation instead.

%% 1.4 Distribution check
% A quality check beyond simple plots: Q-Q plots and the Shapiro-Wilk
% normality test, to guide later decisions about transformations and
% correlation methods. MATLAB has no built-in Shapiro-Wilk test (neither
% base nor the Statistics Toolbox ship one), so swtest.m (Ben Saida,
% 2009/2014, MATLAB File Exchange #13964) is used - it implements
% Royston's AS R94 approximation, matching scipy.stats.shapiro/R's
% shapiro.test to machine precision, EXCEPT that for leptokurtic
% variables (kurtosis > 3) it automatically substitutes the
% Shapiro-Francia test instead (Royston's own recommendation - see the
% function's help text), which Python/R's calls never do. In this
% dataset that affects att_matr, p300_amp and p300_lat - the W/p values
% printed for those three will differ from the Python/R notebooks (same
% conclusion, different exact numbers); all other variables match
% exactly.

fig_dist = figure("Position", [0 0 1600 1100]);
for i = 1:numel(vars)
  col = vars{i};
  v = df.(col);
  row = floor((i - 1) / 5) * 2;

  subplot(4, 5, row * 5 + mod(i - 1, 5) + 1);
  histogram(v, 10);
  hold on;
  yl = ylim();
  plot([mean(v, "omitnan") mean(v, "omitnan")], yl, "r--", "LineWidth", 1.2);
  plot([median(v, "omitnan") median(v, "omitnan")], yl, "g:", "LineWidth", 1.2);
  title(sprintf("%s (n=%d)", col, numel(v)), "Interpreter", "none");
  xlabel(col, "Interpreter", "none"); ylabel("Frequency");

  subplot(4, 5, (row + 1) * 5 + mod(i - 1, 5) + 1);
  qqplot(v);
  title("Q-Q plot");
end

fprintf("Normality tests (Shapiro-Wilk, Shapiro-Francia if leptokurtic):\n");
for i = 1:numel(vars)
  col = vars{i};
  v = df.(col);
  [~, p, W] = swtest(v);
  test_used = "Shapiro-Wilk";
  if kurtosis(v) > 3; test_used = "Shapiro-Francia"; end
  fprintf("  %-10s: n=%d, mean=%.2f, SD=%.2f, W=%.4f, p=%.4f, skew=%.3f, kurt=%.3f (%s)\n", ...
          col, numel(v), mean(v, "omitnan"), std(v, "omitnan"), W, p, skewness(v), kurtosis(v) - 3, test_used);
end

% What do we see in the plot?
%   Histogram - a roughly symmetric, bell-shaped curve suggests
%   normality. Strong skewness or a U-shape would be a warning sign.
%   Q-Q plot - points should fall along the diagonal line if the data
%   are normally distributed.
%
% Interpretation: all Shapiro-Wilk tests are non-significant (p > 0.05)
% and skewness values are well below |0.6|, so the variables are
% approximately normal. Minor scatter in the Q-Q plots is expected with
% n = 40 and does not indicate a problem.

%% 1.5 Outlier detection
% Flag values beyond +-3 standard deviations.

out_mask = false(n_subj, numel(vars));
fprintf("Outliers (+-3 SD):\n");
found_any = false;
for i = 1:numel(vars)
  col = vars{i};
  v = df.(col);
  z = (v - mean(v, "omitnan")) / std(v, "omitnan");
  flagged = find(abs(z) > 3);
  out_mask(flagged, i) = true;
  if ~isempty(flagged)
    found_any = true;
    fprintf("  %s: rows %s\n", col, mat2str(flagged'));
    for r = flagged'
      fprintf("    row %d: %s = %g\n", r, col, v(r));
    end
  end
end
if ~found_any
  fprintf("  None detected.\n");
end

%% 1.6 Cleaning dataset
% Let's remove the missing data and the outliers.
%
% There are three outliers that are not plausible data: Age 150, N400
% Amplitude 25 uV, P300 latency 900ms. We will remove these subjects.
%
% However the value of 3 for attentive matrices is very low but it is
% also very plausible in a patient dataset, therefore we will keep this
% outlier.

missing_mask = any(miss_mat, 2);

% Outliers: exclude only the implausible ones found in Section 1.5 - keep
% the att_matr outlier, since it is a plausible (if low) clinical value
implausible_cols = {'age', 'n400_amp', 'p300_lat'};
[~, implausible_idx] = ismember(implausible_cols, vars);
outlier_mask = any(out_mask(:, implausible_idx), 2);

exclude_mask = missing_mask | outlier_mask;
fprintf("Excluding %d participants:\n", sum(exclude_mask));
disp(df(exclude_mask, [{'subject_id'}, vars]));

df = df(~exclude_mask, :);
n_subj = height(df);
fprintf("\nRemaining: %d participants\n", n_subj);

%% 2. Analysis
%% 2.1 Descriptive statistics (Table 1)

table1_names = vars';
table1_n = zeros(numel(vars), 1);
table1_value = strings(numel(vars), 1);
table1_range = strings(numel(vars), 1);
for i = 1:numel(vars)
  v = df.(vars{i});
  table1_n(i) = numel(v);
  table1_value(i) = sprintf("%.2f +/- %.2f", mean(v), std(v));
  table1_range(i) = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", min(v), max(v));
end
table1 = table(table1_names, table1_n, table1_value, table1_range, ...
  'VariableNames', {'Variable', 'n', 'Value', 'Range'});
disp("Table 1 - Descriptive statistics:");
disp(table1);

%% 2.2 Bivariate correlations (ERP x NPSY)
% Pearson correlations between all variables, with significance stars
% (* p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001).

n_vars = numel(vars);
corr_mat = eye(n_vars);
p_mat = ones(n_vars);
for i = 1:n_vars
  for j = 1:n_vars
    if i == j; continue; end
    x = df.(vars{i}); y = df.(vars{j});
    [r, p] = corr(x, y);
    corr_mat(i, j) = r;
    p_mat(i, j) = p;
  end
end

fig_corr = figure("Position", [0 0 800 700]);
mask = triu(true(n_vars), 1);  % upper triangle, matching the Python/R plot
imagesc(corr_mat, "AlphaData", ~mask);
set(gca, "Color", [1 1 1]);  % masked cells show through as white
clim([-1 1]);
colormap(redblue_colormap());
colorbar();
set(gca, "XTick", 1:n_vars, "XTickLabel", vars, "XTickLabelRotation", 45, ...
         "YTick", 1:n_vars, "YTickLabel", vars, "TickLabelInterpreter", "none");
axis square;
for i = 1:n_vars
  for j = 1:n_vars
    if mask(i, j); continue; end
    r = corr_mat(i, j); p = p_mat(i, j);
    star = "";
    if p < 0.001; star = "***"; elseif p < 0.01; star = "**"; elseif p < 0.05; star = "*"; end
    text(j, i, sprintf("%.3f\n%s", r, star), "HorizontalAlignment", "center", "FontSize", 7);
  end
end
title("Pearson correlations  (* p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001)");

% What do we see in the plot?
%   Each cell shows the Pearson correlation coefficient (r) between a
%   pair of variables. Colours indicate direction: red = positive,
%   blue = negative. Stars indicate significance: * p<0.05, ** p<0.01,
%   *** p<0.001.

%% Key hypothesised associations
% Based on the literature, we focus on two key pairs and plot scatter
% plots with regression lines and 95% confidence bands.

pair_x = {"p300_amp", "n400_lat"};
pair_y = {"att_matr", "apacs"};

fig_scatter = figure("Position", [0 0 1100 450]);
for i = 1:2
  subplot(1, 2, i);
  x = df.(pair_x{i}); y = df.(pair_y{i});
  scatter(x, y, 30, [0.3 0.5 0.8], "filled", "MarkerFaceAlpha", 0.6);
  hold on;

  mdl = fitlm(x, y);
  xg = linspace(min(x), max(x), 100)';
  [yhat, yci] = predict(mdl, xg);
  fill([xg; flipud(xg)], [yci(:, 1); flipud(yci(:, 2))], ...
       [0 0.47 0.42], "FaceAlpha", 0.15, "EdgeColor", "none");
  plot(xg, yhat, "Color", [0 0.47 0.42], "LineWidth", 1.5);

  [r, p] = corr(x, y);
  title(sprintf("%s vs %s   r=%.3f, p=%.4f", pair_x{i}, pair_y{i}, r, p), "Interpreter", "none");
  xlabel(pair_x{i}, "Interpreter", "none"); ylabel(pair_y{i}, "Interpreter", "none");
end

% What do we see in the plot?
%   Each dot is one participant. The regression line shows the best-fit
%   linear relationship; the shaded band is the 95% confidence interval.
%   r quantifies strength (-1 to +1); p tests whether it is
%   significantly different from zero.

%% 2.3 General linear models
% Three models, mirroring the Python/R versions:
%   - APACS (theory-driven): apacs ~ n400_lat + n400_amp + age
%   - Attentive Matrices (kitchen-sink, no a priori knowledge): all
%     covariates thrown in, to illustrate the cost of ignoring theory
%   - Attentive Matrices (parsimonious, theory-guided):
%     att_matr ~ p300_amp + age + criq, with predictors chosen a priori
%     from theory and the Section 2.2 correlations, not by trimming
%     non-significant terms from the kitchen-sink model (that would be
%     post-hoc pruning, a form of circular reasoning).

mod_apacs = fitlm(df, "apacs ~ n400_lat + n400_amp + age");
disp("APACS (theory-driven):"); disp(mod_apacs);

mod_att_matr_full = fitlm(df, "att_matr ~ p300_lat + p300_amp + n400_lat + n400_amp + age + sex + criq");
disp("Attentive Matrices (kitchen-sink):"); disp(mod_att_matr_full);

mod_att_matr_pars = fitlm(df, "att_matr ~ p300_amp + age + criq");
disp("Attentive Matrices (parsimonious):"); disp(mod_att_matr_pars);

% Takeaway: more variables does not mean a better model. The predictors
% in the parsimonious model were chosen a priori, from theory and from
% the Section 2.2 correlations, before looking at any p-value from the
% kitchen-sink model - the kitchen-sink model exists only to illustrate
% the cost of ignoring theory (inflated standard errors, an unstable
% intercept), not to guide which variables to keep.

%% 2.4 Assumption checking (post-hoc)
% Checked here for the final, parsimonious Attentive Matrices model.

mod = mod_att_matr_pars;
fitted = mod.Fitted; resid = mod.Residuals.Raw; n = mod.NumObservations;
cooks = mod.Diagnostics.CooksDistance;

fig_diag = figure("Position", [0 0 1000 800]);

subplot(2, 2, 1);
scatter(fitted, resid, 25, [0.3 0.5 0.8], "filled");
hold on; plot(xlim(), [0 0], "k--");
xlabel("Fitted values"); ylabel("Residuals"); title("Residuals vs Fitted");

subplot(2, 2, 2);
qqplot(resid);
title("Q-Q plot (residuals)");

subplot(2, 2, 3);
stem(1:n, cooks, "filled", "MarkerSize", 3);
hold on;
thresh = 4 / n;
h_thresh = plot(xlim(), [thresh thresh], "r--");
xlabel("Participant (row index)"); ylabel("Cook's distance");
title("Cook's Distance");
legend(h_thresh, sprintf("4/n = %.3f", thresh), "Location", "best");

subplot(2, 2, 4);
% Classic VIF formula: diagonal of the inverse correlation matrix of the
% predictors (equivalent to 1 / (1 - R^2) from the auxiliary regressions).
vif_names = {"p300_amp", "age", "criq"};
X = [df.p300_amp, df.age, df.criq];
vifs = diag(inv(corrcoef(X)));
barh(1:3, vifs, "FaceColor", [0.27 0.51 0.71]);
set(gca, "YTick", 1:3, "YTickLabel", vif_names, "TickLabelInterpreter", "none");
hold on;
h_vif5 = plot([5 5], ylim(), "Color", [1 0.55 0], "LineStyle", "--");
h_vif10 = plot([10 10], ylim(), "r--");
xlabel("VIF"); title("Variance Inflation Factor");
legend([h_vif5, h_vif10], {"VIF=5", "VIF=10"}, "Location", "best");

fprintf("\n  predictor      VIF\n");
for i = 1:3
  fprintf("  %-10s %.6f\n", vif_names{i}, vifs(i));
end
n_influential = sum(cooks > 4 / n);
fprintf("\nParticipants above the 4/n Cook's distance threshold: %d (max Cook's D = %.3f)\n", ...
        n_influential, max(cooks));

% What do we see in the plot?
%   Residuals vs Fitted - no funnel shape or curve should be visible.
%   Q-Q plot (residuals) - points should lie close to the diagonal.
%   Cook's distance - a handful of points above the 4/n line is not
%   unusual with n = 40 and is not, on its own, a red flag.
%   VIF - values close to 1 mean each predictor carries mostly
%   independent information; all three sit well below VIF = 5.
%
% Interpretation: diagnostics are reassuring for the parsimonious
% Attentive Matrices model - residuals show no obvious pattern, the Q-Q
% plot is close to the diagonal, no participant has a disproportionately
% large Cook's distance, and VIF values are low.

%% 3. Export
%% 3.1 Figures

figures_to_save = struct( ...
  "A_missingness", fig_missing, ...
  "B_distributions", fig_dist, ...
  "C_correlations", fig_corr, ...
  "D_key_associations", fig_scatter, ...
  "E_diagnostics_attentive_matrices", fig_diag);
fn = fieldnames(figures_to_save);
for i = 1:numel(fn)
  path = fullfile(FIGS, [fn{i} '.png']);
  exportgraphics(figures_to_save.(fn{i}), path, 'Resolution', 150);
  fprintf("Saved: %s\n", path);
end

%% 3.2 Tables

writetable(table1, fullfile(RESULTS, "table1_descriptives.csv"));

% Table 2 - bivariate correlations, one row per unique pair
t2_v1 = strings(0, 1); t2_v2 = strings(0, 1); t2_r = []; t2_p = []; t2_sig = logical([]);
for i = 1:n_vars
  for j = (i+1):n_vars
    t2_v1(end+1, 1) = vars{i};
    t2_v2(end+1, 1) = vars{j};
    t2_r(end+1, 1) = corr_mat(i, j);
    t2_p(end+1, 1) = p_mat(i, j);
    t2_sig(end+1, 1) = p_mat(i, j) < 0.05;
  end
end
table2 = table(t2_v1, t2_v2, t2_r, t2_p, t2_sig, ...
  'VariableNames', {'Variable_1', 'Variable_2', 'r', 'p_value', 'Significant_p_05'});
writetable(table2, fullfile(RESULTS, "table2_correlations.csv"));

% Table 3 - regression coefficients for all three fitted models
t3_outcome = strings(0, 1); t3_pred = strings(0, 1);
t3_est = []; t3_se = []; t3_p = []; t3_lo = []; t3_hi = []; t3_sig = logical([]);
models = {mod_apacs, mod_att_matr_full, mod_att_matr_pars};
labels = {"APACS (theory-driven)", "Attentive Matrices (kitchen-sink)", "Attentive Matrices (parsimonious)"};
for m = 1:3
  fit = models{m};
  ci = coefCI(fit);
  coef_names = fit.CoefficientNames;
  for i = 1:numel(coef_names)
    t3_outcome(end+1, 1) = labels{m};
    t3_pred(end+1, 1) = coef_names{i};
    t3_est(end+1, 1) = fit.Coefficients.Estimate(i);
    t3_se(end+1, 1) = fit.Coefficients.SE(i);
    t3_p(end+1, 1) = fit.Coefficients.pValue(i);
    t3_lo(end+1, 1) = ci(i, 1);
    t3_hi(end+1, 1) = ci(i, 2);
    t3_sig(end+1, 1) = fit.Coefficients.pValue(i) < 0.05;
  end
end
table3 = table(t3_outcome, t3_pred, t3_est, t3_se, t3_p, t3_lo, t3_hi, t3_sig, ...
  'VariableNames', {'Outcome', 'Predictor', 'Estimate', 'Std_Error', 'p_value', 'CI_lower', 'CI_upper', 'Significant_p_05'});
writetable(table3, fullfile(RESULTS, "table3_regression.csv"));

% Table 4 - VIF (Attentive Matrices, parsimonious model)
table4 = table(vif_names', vifs, 'VariableNames', {'Predictor', 'VIF'});
writetable(table4, fullfile(RESULTS, "table4_vif.csv"));

fprintf("Saved 4 result tables to %s\n", RESULTS);

% Also export everything to a single Excel workbook, one sheet per table -
% writetable infers the format from the extension, no extra toolbox needed.
xlsx_path = fullfile(RESULTS, "CaseStudy_1_results.xlsx");
writetable(table1, xlsx_path, "Sheet", "descriptives");
writetable(table2, xlsx_path, "Sheet", "correlations");
writetable(table3, xlsx_path, "Sheet", "regression");
writetable(table4, xlsx_path, "Sheet", "vif");
fprintf("Saved: %s\n", xlsx_path);

%% 4. Strengths and limitations of this approach (Section 4.2.3)
%
% Strengths:
%   - Reduces high-dimensional EEG to 4 interpretable scalar features
%     per participant - theoretically grounded, easy to communicate
%   - Uses well-established statistical models (OLS regression) familiar
%     to clinical researchers
%   - The N400 and P300 have decades of validation across neurological
%     populations (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Polich, 2007)
%
% Limitations:
%   - Strong a priori decisions about time windows and electrode sets
%     may miss atypical or distributed neural patterns
%   - Trial-to-trial variability is discarded (only mean amplitude and
%     peak latency are kept), which may itself carry clinically relevant
%     information
%   - The hypothesis-driven nature of the approach means it will not
%     detect effects outside the predefined features - for broader
%     exploration, see Case Study 2 (spectral analysis)
%
% For a full discussion, see Section 4.2 of the companion paper.
%
% Generated for the EEG-NPSY tutorial. All code is self-contained for
% transparency and reproducibility.

What do we see in the plot?

Histogram — a roughly symmetric, bell-shaped curve suggests normality. Strong skewness (long tail to one side) or a U-shape would be a warning sign.

Q-Q plot — points should fall along the diagonal line if the data are normally distributed. Key departures:

Both ends curve away from the line → heavy tails (more extreme values than a normal distribution would predict)

S-shaped curve → skewed distribution (left-skewed if the curve goes below then above the line; right-skewed if the reverse)

Points deviating in the middle only → unusual peakedness (kurtosis)

This theory-guided model has fewer predictors, and — as a consequence, not as the reason we chose them — all of them are significant and the model is more stable. Because the selection was made a priori rather than by trimming non-significant terms, the improved fit (comparable or better R² with fewer parameters) can be read as genuine evidence in favour of parsimony, rather than as an artefact of having searched the data for whichever subset happens to look best.

Takeaway

More variables does not mean a better model — and how you choose which variables to drop matters just as much as the decision to drop them. Selecting predictors after seeing that they are not significant in a bigger model is a form of post hoc pruning, which is circular: the same data end up being used both to choose the model and to test it, which inflates the apparent evidence for whatever predictors remain.

Here the predictors were instead chosen a priori, from theory and from the earlier correlation analysis (Section 2.2), before looking at any p-value from the kitchen-sink model. The kitchen-sink model was fit only to illustrate the cost of ignoring theory — inflated standard errors, an unstable intercept — not to guide which variables to keep. That the resulting theory-driven model also turns out to fit at least as well (higher pseudo R², all coefficients significant, and a simpler, more interpretable structure) is a welcome confirmation, not the justification for the choice.

Participants above the 4/n Cook's distance threshold: 3 (max Cook's D = 0.236)

What do we see in the plot?

Residuals vs Fitted — no funnel shape or curve should be visible; a random scatter around zero supports linearity and constant variance (homoscedasticity).

Q-Q plot (residuals) — points should lie close to the diagonal; systematic curvature would suggest non-normal errors.

Cook's distance — a handful of points above the 4/n line is not unusual with n = 40 and, on its own, is not a red flag: what matters is whether any point stands out with a much larger value than the rest (a useful check is to refit the model without that participant and see whether the coefficients change materially).

VIF — values close to 1 mean each predictor carries mostly independent information; here p300_amp, age, and criq all sit well below the VIF = 5 caution threshold, so multicollinearity is not a concern for this model.

Interpretation: for the parsimonious Attentive Matrices model, the diagnostics are reassuring — residuals show no obvious pattern, the Q-Q plot is close to the diagonal, no participant has a disproportionately large Cook's distance, and VIF values are low. This supports treating the model's coefficients (Section 2.3) at face value.

docs.title: Case Study 1 — Analytical strategy based on reduced EEG features¶
docs.text:
This case study implements the analysis described in Section 4.1 of the companion paper.

The research question is:

Are the amplitude and latency of specific ERP components associated with neuropsychological performance and demographic characteristics in post-stroke patients?

Two well-characterised ERP components are used:

  • N400 — a negative deflection ~400 ms post-stimulus, indexing semantice processing (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011)
  • P300 — a positive deflection ~300 ms post-target, indexing attentional resource allocation (Polich, 2007)

From each component we consider amplitude (mean µV within a predefined time window) and latency (ms of peak amplitude), yielding four participant-level neural predictors.

As it usually happens in real life, data are delivered in two different files: dataset_NPSY.csv and dataset_ERP.csv.

docs.title: Pipeline¶
docs.text:
1. Data Wrangling — load, inspect, check ranges, missing data, distributions, outliers, multicollinearity
  2. Analysis — descriptive stats, bivariate correlations, multiple regression, diagnostics, multiple comparison correction
  3. Export — save tables and figures

All code is defined directly here for transparency and reproducibility. Each step is explained as we go.

docs.title: 0. Setup¶
docs.text: Import the libraries we will use throughout the analysis.

docs.title: 1.1 Load data¶
docs.text: The datasets are stored as separate CSV files linked by subject_id.

docs.title: 1.2 Initial inspection¶
docs.text:
We check dataset dimensions, column types, and basic descriptive statistics.

Expected clinical ranges:

Variable Expected range Age 18–100 years CRIq 70–130 N400 amplitude 1–6 µV N400 latency 350–500 ms P300 amplitude 5–20 µV P300 latency 300–500 ms APACS 0–1 Attentive Matrices 0–60 MoCA 0–30

docs.title: 1.3 Missing data¶
docs.text:
Missing data are common in clinical neuropsychological datasets — they can arise from fatigue, incomplete testing, or participant dropout. Strategies include:

  • Listwise deletion (exclude participants with any missing value) — simple, but reduces sample size and may bias estimates if data are not missing completely at random (MCAR).
  • Multiple imputation (e.g., MICE) — preserves sample size and is valid under the weaker assumption of missing at random (MAR). Generally preferred in clinical samples.

Our synthetic dataset has complete data for 40 participants, 2 participants with missing data and 3 with outliers.

Visual inspection of missing data patterns:

docs.title: 1.4 Distribution check¶
docs.text: More than just plotting the data we can already perform a quality check by looking at the Q-Q plots, and running the Shapiro-Wilk normality test. This guides later decisions about transformations and correlation methods.

docs.title: 1.5 Outlier detection¶
docs.text: Flag values beyond ±3 standard deviations. We inspect flagged cases and note whether they are data-entry errors or genuine extremes.

docs.title: 1.6 Cleaning dataset¶
docs.text:
Let's remove the missing data and the outliers.

There are three outliers that are not plausible data: Age 150, N400 Amplitude 25 uV, P300 latitude 900ms. We will then remove this subjects.

However the value of 3 for attentive matrices is very low but it is also very plausible in a patient dataset, therefore we will keep this outlier.

docs.title: 2.1 Descriptive statistics (Table 1)¶
docs.text: We describe each variable by looking at its mean, standard deviation, and range of values

docs.title: 2.2 Bivariate correlations (ERP × NPSY)¶
docs.text: We compute Pearson correlations between all the variables, but the interesting values are the ones between the ERP features and the neuropsychological outcomes. The heatmap shows r values with significance stars (* p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001).

docs.title: Key hypothesised associations¶
docs.text: Based on the literature, we focus on two key pairs and generate scatter plots with regression lines and 95 % confidence bands.

docs.title: 2.3 General linear models¶
docs.text: We fit three models, each with a different structure. This reflects the reality of clinical research: sometimes we have a clear theoretical prediction, sometimes we explore, and sometimes we learn from our mistakes and simplify.

docs.title: APACS - A theory-driven model¶
docs.text:
Descrizione di modello teorico per APACS

APACS ~ N400_lat + N400_amp + Age

docs.title: Attentive Matrices - A model with no a priori knowledge¶
docs.text:
Now we want to build a model for attentive matrices.

As known by the theory, and also shown in the previous correlation plot, attentive matrices are correlated to P300, education (CRIq), and age.

But our dataset includes much more variables, therefore one idea could be bigger is better: let's put everything together

So we can try to fit a kitchen-sink model using all the data as covariates: AttentiveMatrices ~ P300_lat + P300_amp + N400_lat + N400_amp + Age + Sex + CRIq

We fit this model only to see what happens when theory is ignored and every available variable is thrown in — not to use its p-values to decide afterwards which variables to keep (see below).

docs.title: Attentive Matrices - A theory-guided, parsimonious model¶
docs.text:
The kitchen-sink model above shows the cost of ignoring theory: several predictors are far from significant, and entering redundant or theoretically unmotivated variables inflates standard errors and destabilises the coefficients.

Importantly, we do not decide which variables to keep by looking at these p-values — that would be post-hoc pruning, a form of circular reasoning: the same data would first be searched to select the model and then reused to test it, inflating the apparent evidence for whatever survives. Instead we go back to theory and to the earlier bivariate analysis (Section 2.2): P300 amplitude, age, and CRIq are the established covariates for attentional performance, so those are the predictors we keep a priori. N400 amplitude/latency and P300 latency are dropped because there is no theoretical reason to expect them to explain attentive matrices performance specifically, and sex is dropped on the same a priori grounds — not because it failed to reach significance above.

Attentive Matrices ~ P300_amp + Age + CRIq

docs.title: 2.4 Assumption checking (post-hoc)¶
docs.text:
Fitting a model is not the last step: linear regression relies on a few assumptions, and good practice is to check them after fitting, before trusting the coefficients. We do this here for the final, parsimonious Attentive Matrices model (att_matr ~ p300_amp + age + criq).

  • Linearity & homoscedasticity — residuals plotted against fitted values should scatter randomly around zero, with no funnel shape or curve.
  • Normality of residuals — a Q-Q plot of the residuals should follow the diagonal (same logic as the Q-Q plots in Section 1.4, now applied to the model's errors instead of the raw variables).
  • Influential observations — Cook's distance flags participants who, on their own, pull the fitted model strongly in one direction. A common rule of thumb is to inspect points above 4/n.
  • Multicollinearity — the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) quantifies how much a predictor's variance is inflated by correlation with the other predictors. VIF > 5 is a moderate concern, VIF > 10 is severe (see Section 1.6 of the pipeline). The intercept is excluded from the VIF table/plot below, since its VIF is a statistical artefact with no interpretation as a collinearity check.

docs.title: 3. Export¶
docs.text:
We now save the results that matter most for a clinical audience: the key figures (as PNG images, ready to paste into a report or a slide) and the key tables (as both .csv — universal, opens anywhere — and .xlsx — a single Excel workbook with one sheet per table, easier to browse for those who are not used to statistical software).

Nothing here is recomputed: we simply save the figures and tables already produced above.

docs.title: 3.1 Figures¶
docs.text: We save the figures produced earlier, one PNG per figure.

docs.title: 3.2 Tables¶
docs.text:
We export four tables:

  1. Descriptive statistics (table1, already built in Section 2.1)
  2. Bivariate correlations — every pair of variables, one row per pair (long/tidy format, easier to filter and sort in Excel than a matrix)
  3. Regression results — coefficients, standard errors, p-values and 95% CI for all three models (APACS, and both Attentive Matrices models)
  4. Multicollinearity check (VIF) — for the parsimonious Attentive Matrices model (Section 2.4)

Each table gets a Significant (p<0.05) column so it is immediately clear, without reading p-values, which associations/predictors reach conventional significance.

docs.title: 4. Strengths and limitations of this approach (Section 4.2.3)¶
docs.text:
Strengths:

  • Reduces high-dimensional EEG to 4 interpretable scalar features per participant — theoretically grounded, easy to communicate
  • Uses well-established statistical models (OLS regression) familiar to clinical researchers
  • The N400 and P300 have decades of validation across neurological populations (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Polich, 2007)

Limitations:

  • Strong a priori decisions about time windows and electrode sets may miss atypical or distributed neural patterns — especially relevant in stroke patients whose ERP topography may differ from normative expectations
  • Trial-to-trial variability is discarded (only mean amplitude and peak latency are kept), which may itself carry clinically relevant information
  • The hypothesis-driven nature of the approach means it will not detect effects outside the predefined features — for broader exploration, see Case Study 2 (spectral analysis)

For a full discussion, see Section 4.2 of the companion paper.

Generated for the EEG-NPSY tutorial. All code is self-contained for transparency and reproducibility.

What do we see in the plot?

Histogram — a roughly symmetric, bell-shaped curve suggests normality. Strong skewness (long tail to one side) or a U-shape would be a warning sign.

Q-Q plot — points should fall along the diagonal line if the data are normally distributed. Key departures:

Both ends curve away from the line → heavy tails (more extreme values than a normal distribution would predict)

S-shaped curve → skewed distribution (left-skewed if the curve goes below then above the line; right-skewed if the reverse)

Points deviating in the middle only → unusual peakedness (kurtosis)

What do we see in the plot?

Each dot shows the values of one participant.

The regression line shows the best-fit linear relationship — upward slope = positive association, flat = none.

The shaded band is the 95 % confidence interval: narrower = more precise estimate, wider = more uncertainty (typically at the extremes). If the band includes a horizontal line, the slope may not be significant.

The r value (Pearson correlation coefficient) quantifies strength (−1 to +1); p tests whether it is significantly different from zero.

This theory-guided model has fewer predictors, and — as a consequence, not as the reason we chose them — all of them are significant and the model is more stable. Because the selection was made a priori rather than by trimming non-significant terms, the improved fit (a lower AIC, despite — in fact because of — fewer parameters) can be read as genuine evidence in favour of parsimony, rather than as an artefact of having searched the data for whichever subset happens to look best.

Takeaway

More variables does not mean a better model — and how you choose which variables to drop matters just as much as the decision to drop them. Selecting predictors after seeing that they are not significant in a bigger model is a form of post hoc pruning, which is circular: the same data end up being used both to choose the model and to test it, which inflates the apparent evidence for whatever predictors remain.

Here the predictors were instead chosen a priori, from theory and from the earlier correlation analysis (Section 2.2), before looking at any p-value from the kitchen-sink model. The kitchen-sink model was fit only to illustrate the cost of ignoring theory — inflated standard errors, an unstable intercept — not to guide which variables to keep. That the resulting theory-driven model also turns out to fit at least as well (a lower AIC, all coefficients significant, and a simpler, more interpretable structure) is a welcome confirmation, not the justification for the choice.

What do we see in the plot?

Residuals vs Fitted — no funnel shape or curve should be visible; a random scatter around zero supports linearity and constant variance (homoscedasticity).

Q-Q plot (residuals) — points should lie close to the diagonal; systematic curvature would suggest non-normal errors.

Cook's distance — a handful of points above the 4/n line is not unusual with n = 40 and, on its own, is not a red flag: what matters is whether any point stands out with a much larger value than the rest (a useful check is to refit the model without that participant and see whether the coefficients change materially).

VIF — values close to 1 mean each predictor carries mostly independent information; here p300_amp, age, and criq all sit well below the VIF = 5 caution threshold, so multicollinearity is not a concern for this model.

Interpretation: for the parsimonious Attentive Matrices model, the diagnostics are reassuring — residuals show no obvious pattern, the Q-Q plot is close to the diagonal, no participant has a disproportionately large Cook's distance, and VIF values are low. This supports treating the model's coefficients (Section 2.3) at face value.

docs.title: Case Study 1 — Analytical strategy based on reduced EEG features (R)¶
docs.text:
This is the R implementation of Case Study 1. It implements the analysis described in Section 4.1 of the companion paper. The same analysis is also available as Python code.

The research question is:

Are the amplitude and latency of specific ERP components associated with neuropsychological performance and demographic characteristics in post-stroke patients?

Two well-characterised ERP components are used:

  • N400 — a negative deflection ~400 ms post-stimulus, indexing semantic processing (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011)
  • P300 — a positive deflection ~300 ms post-target, indexing attentional resource allocation (Polich, 2007)

From each component we consider amplitude (mean µV within a predefined time window) and latency (ms of peak amplitude), yielding four participant-level neural predictors.

As it usually happens in real life, data are delivered in two different files: dataset_NPSY.csv and dataset_ERP.csv.

docs.title: Pipeline¶
docs.text:
1. Data Wrangling — load, inspect, check ranges, missing data, distributions, outliers
  2. Analysis — descriptive stats, bivariate correlations, multiple regression, post-hoc diagnostics
  3. Export — save tables and figures

All code is defined directly here for transparency and reproducibility. Each step is explained as we go.

docs.title: 0. Setup¶
docs.text: Import the libraries we will use throughout the analysis.

docs.title: 1.1 Load data¶
docs.text: The datasets are stored as separate CSV files linked by subject_id.

docs.title: 1.2 Initial inspection¶
docs.text:
We check dataset dimensions, column types, and basic descriptive statistics.

Expected clinical ranges:

Variable Expected range Age 18–100 years CRIq 70–130 N400 amplitude 1–6 µV N400 latency 350–500 ms P300 amplitude 5–20 µV P300 latency 300–500 ms APACS 0–1 Attentive Matrices 0–60 MoCA 0–30

docs.title: 1.3 Missing data¶
docs.text:
Missing data are common in clinical neuropsychological datasets — they can arise from fatigue, incomplete testing, or participant dropout. Strategies include:

  • Listwise deletion (exclude participants with any missing value) — simple, but reduces sample size and may bias estimates if data are not missing completely at random (MCAR).
  • Multiple imputation (e.g., MICE, see the mice package) — preserves sample size and is valid under the weaker assumption of missing at random (MAR). Generally preferred in clinical samples.

Our synthetic dataset has complete data for all 40 participants, so no imputation is needed here. The code below would work with either scenario.

Visual inspection of missing data patterns:

docs.title: 1.4 Distribution check¶
docs.text: More than just plotting the data we can already perform a quality check by looking at the Q-Q plots, and running the Shapiro-Wilk normality test. This guides later decisions about transformations and correlation methods.

docs.title: 1.5 Outlier detection¶
docs.text: Flag values beyond ±3 standard deviations. We inspect flagged cases and note whether they are data-entry errors or genuine extremes.

docs.title: 1.6 Cleaning dataset¶
docs.text:
Let's remove the missing data and the outliers.

There are three outliers that are not plausible data: Age 150, N400 Amplitude 25 uV, P300 latency 900ms. We will remove these subjects.

However the value of 3 for attentive matrices is very low but it is also very plausible in a patient dataset, therefore we will keep this outlier.

docs.title: 2.1 Descriptive statistics (Table 1)¶
docs.text: We describe each variable by looking at its mean, standard deviation, and range of values

docs.title: 2.2 Bivariate correlations (ERP × NPSY)¶
docs.text: We compute Pearson correlations between all the variables, but the interesting values are the ones between the ERP features and the neuropsychological outcomes. The heatmap shows r values with significance stars (* p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001).

docs.title: Key hypothesised associations¶
docs.text: Based on the literature, we focus on two key pairs and generate scatter plots with regression lines and 95 % confidence bands.

docs.title: 2.3 General linear models¶
docs.text: We fit three models, each with a different structure. This reflects the reality of clinical research: sometimes we have a clear theoretical prediction, sometimes we explore, and sometimes we learn from our mistakes and simplify.

docs.title: APACS - A theory-driven model¶
docs.text:
Descrizione di modello teorico per APACS

APACS ~ N400_lat + N400_amp + Age

docs.title: Attentive Matrices - A model with no a priori knowledge¶
docs.text:
Now we want to build a model for attentive matrices.

As known by the theory, and also shown in the previous correlation plot, attentive matrices are correlated to P300, education (CRIq), and age.

But our dataset includes much more variables, therefore one idea could be bigger is better: let's put everything together

So we can try to fit a kitchen-sink model using all the data as covariates: AttentiveMatrices ~ P300_lat + P300_amp + N400_lat + N400_amp + Age + Sex + CRIq

We fit this model only to see what happens when theory is ignored and every available variable is thrown in — not to use its p-values to decide afterwards which variables to keep (see below).

docs.title: Attentive Matrices - A theory-guided, parsimonious model¶
docs.text:
The kitchen-sink model above shows the cost of ignoring theory: several predictors are far from significant, and entering redundant or theoretically unmotivated variables inflates standard errors and destabilises the coefficients.

Importantly, we do not decide which variables to keep by looking at these p-values — that would be post-hoc pruning, a form of circular reasoning: the same data would first be searched to select the model and then reused to test it, inflating the apparent evidence for whatever survives. Instead we go back to theory and to the earlier bivariate analysis (Section 2.2): P300 amplitude, age, and CRIq are the established covariates for attentional performance, so those are the predictors we keep a priori. N400 amplitude/latency and P300 latency are dropped because there is no theoretical reason to expect them to explain attentive matrices performance specifically, and sex is dropped on the same a priori grounds — not because it failed to reach significance above.

Attentive Matrices ~ P300_amp + Age + CRIq

docs.title: 2.4 Assumption checking (post-hoc)¶
docs.text:
Fitting a model is not the last step: linear regression relies on a few assumptions, and good practice is to check them after fitting, before trusting the coefficients. We do this here for the final, parsimonious Attentive Matrices model (att_matr ~ p300_amp + age + criq).

  • Linearity & homoscedasticity — residuals plotted against fitted values should scatter randomly around zero, with no funnel shape or curve.
  • Normality of residuals — a Q-Q plot of the residuals should follow the diagonal (same logic as the Q-Q plots in Section 1.4, now applied to the model's errors instead of the raw variables).
  • Influential observations — Cook's distance flags participants who, on their own, pull the fitted model strongly in one direction. A common rule of thumb is to inspect points above 4/n.
  • Multicollinearity — the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) quantifies how much a predictor's variance is inflated by correlation with the other predictors. VIF > 5 is a moderate concern, VIF > 10 is severe. Unlike a manual VIF calculation, R's car::vif() never includes the intercept in the first place, so there is nothing to exclude here.

docs.title: 3. Export¶
docs.text:
We now save the results that matter most for a clinical audience: the key figures (as PNG images, ready to paste into a report or a slide) and the key tables (as both .csv — universal, opens anywhere — and .xlsx — a single Excel workbook with one sheet per table, easier to browse for those who are not used to statistical software).

Nothing here is recomputed: we simply save the figures and tables already produced above.

docs.title: 3.1 Figures¶
docs.text: We save the figures produced earlier, one PNG per figure.

docs.title: 3.2 Tables¶
docs.text:
We export four tables:

  1. Descriptive statistics (table1, already built in Section 2.1)
  2. Bivariate correlations — every pair of variables, one row per pair (long/tidy format, easier to filter and sort in Excel than a matrix)
  3. Regression results — coefficients, standard errors, p-values and 95% CI for all three models (APACS, and both Attentive Matrices models)
  4. Multicollinearity check (VIF) — for the parsimonious Attentive Matrices model (Section 2.4)

Each table gets a Significant (p<0.05) column so it is immediately clear, without reading p-values, which associations/predictors reach conventional significance.

docs.title: 4. Strengths and limitations of this approach (Section 4.2.3)¶
docs.text:
Strengths:

  • Reduces high-dimensional EEG to 4 interpretable scalar features per participant — theoretically grounded, easy to communicate
  • Uses well-established statistical models (OLS regression) familiar to clinical researchers
  • The N400 and P300 have decades of validation across neurological populations (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Polich, 2007)

Limitations:

  • Strong a priori decisions about time windows and electrode sets may miss atypical or distributed neural patterns — especially relevant in stroke patients whose ERP topography may differ from normative expectations
  • Trial-to-trial variability is discarded (only mean amplitude and peak latency are kept), which may itself carry clinically relevant information
  • The hypothesis-driven nature of the approach means it will not detect effects outside the predefined features — for broader exploration, see Case Study 2 (spectral analysis)

For a full discussion, see Section 4.2 of the companion paper.

def partial_corr_tmap(log_power, y, age, criq, n_ch_, n_freq_):
    # partial-correlation t-map of log_power vs y, controlling age & criq
    n = len(y)
    Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), age, criq])
    Z_pinv = np.linalg.pinv(Z)
    resid_y = y - Z @ (Z_pinv @ y)
    Y = log_power.reshape(n, -1)
    resid_power = Y - Z @ (Z_pinv @ Y)
    num = resid_y @ resid_power
    den = np.sqrt((resid_y ** 2).sum()) * np.sqrt((resid_power ** 2).sum(axis=0))
    r = np.clip(num / den, -0.999999, 0.999999)
    df = n - 4   # n - intercept - age - criq - y
    t = r * np.sqrt(df / (1 - r ** 2))
    return t.reshape(n_ch_, n_freq_)

def find_clusters(t_map, t_thresh, adjacency):
    flat = t_map.reshape(-1)
    clusters = []
    for sign in (1, -1):
        supra = (flat * sign) > t_thresh
        if not supra.any():
            continue
        sub_adj = adjacency[supra][:, supra]
        n_comp, labels = connected_components(sub_adj, directed=False)
        idx_supra = np.where(supra)[0]
        for comp in range(n_comp):
            members = idx_supra[labels == comp]
            clusters.append((members, flat[members].sum()))
    return clusters


def cluster_permutation_test(log_power, y, age, criq, adjacency, n_ch_, n_freq_,
                              t_thresh=2.028, n_perm=2000, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t_obs = partial_corr_tmap(log_power, y, age, criq, n_ch_, n_freq_)
    obs_clusters = sorted(find_clusters(t_obs, t_thresh, adjacency), key=lambda c: -abs(c[1]))
    null_max = np.zeros(n_perm)
    for i in range(n_perm):
        shuffled = rng.permutation(len(y))
        t_perm = partial_corr_tmap(log_power, y[shuffled], age, criq, n_ch_, n_freq_)
        cl = find_clusters(t_perm, t_thresh, adjacency)
        null_max[i] = max((abs(m) for _, m in cl), default=0.0)
    results = []
    for members, mass in obs_clusters[:5]:
        p = (null_max >= abs(mass)).mean()
        results.append({"members": members, "mass": mass, "p_cluster": p})
    return results, t_obs

What do we see in the plots?

Each panel is one canonical band, coloured by the same t-value scale; a panel's channels would be marked if that band's cluster survived correction for having tested five bands. This is a noticeably messier picture than a clean "low frequencies yes, high frequencies no" split: none of the five individual bands survives Bonferroni correction (theta comes closest, at a raw p≈0.03 that is no longer below 0.05 once multiplied by 5), even though several bands show the same right-lateralised, negative direction as the pre-registered secondary test above.

This is a more informative result than a clean split would have been, for two reasons. First, it is a direct, concrete illustration of why multiple-comparison correction matters: taken on its own, theta's raw p-value would look like a finding — it only stops looking like one once we account for having tested five bands instead of pre-committing to one. Second, it shows why the secondary analysis pooled delta and theta together rather than testing them separately: combining adjacent frequency bins into one wider band gives the cluster more points to draw statistical mass from, which is exactly what recovers the significant result there. Splitting the spectrum into ever-narrower slices trades away the power that made the pooled test work in the first place — the same lesson Case Study 1 taught about predictors, now shown for frequency bands.

docs.title: Case Study 2 — Whole-scalp spectral analysis of resting-state EEG¶
docs.text:
This case study implements the analysis described in Section 4.2 of the companion paper.

The research question is:

Does the spectral profile of resting-state EEG relate to global cognitive functioning, without restricting the analysis in advance to a specific frequency band or region?

Where Case Study 1 reduces the EEG signal to four theory-driven scalar features, this case study keeps the full power spectral density (PSD, 1–40 Hz, every channel) and asks broadly where — across the whole scalp and spectrum — resting EEG power relates to global cognition (MoCA), motivated by a well-established clinical observation: right-hemisphere stroke is frequently accompanied by pathological EEG slowing (more delta/theta power over the affected region) that tracks the severity of impairment (Finnigan & Van Putten, 2013).

docs.title: A note on the data¶
docs.text:
• The EEG spectra used here are real, anonymised recordings..
  • The neuropsychological table (age, sex, CRIq, MoCA) is synthetic, as in Case Study 1.
  • Because the two do not come from the same assessment, the moca column was deliberately linked to a real, montage-based property of each EEG recording — see the notice at the top of data/generate_datasets.ipynb for the full disclosure. The resulting brain–behaviour association should not be read as a real clinical finding; it exists so this case study has something real to recover.

docs.title: Pipeline¶
docs.text:
1. Data Wrangling — load & align, inspect, missing data, log-power distributions, covariate strategy
  2. Analysis — descriptive stats, a Case-Study-1-style baseline model, mass-univariate partial correlation, cluster-based permutation (primary whole-spectrum test + a pre-registered secondary/confirmatory test)
  3. Export — figures and tables (CSV + Excel)
  4. Strengths and limitations

This analysis needs more than Case Study 1: mne for electrode positions, spatial adjacency, and topographic plots.

docs.title: 1.1 Load data¶
docs.text: The EEG spectra are stored as a [subjects x channels x frequencies] array, linked to the neuropsychological table by subject_id. Unlike Case Study 1's CSV files, this is too large for a spreadsheet — it comes as three companion files (the array, the channel names, the frequency axis).

docs.title: 1.2 Missing data and outliers¶
docs.text: As in Case Study 1 (see its Sections 1.3-1.6 for the full walk-through), a few participants have missing or implausible values. Since this is the same dataset, we exclude the same subjects here before any further inspection.

docs.title: 1.3 Initial inspection¶
docs.text: A quick sanity check before anything else: does the grand-average spectrum look like a real EEG spectrum (1/f-like decay, no obvious line noise or flat channels)?

docs.title: 1.4 Log-power distribution check¶
docs.text: The PSD array is already log-transformed (log-power is approximately normally distributed, whereas raw spectral power is strongly right- skewed — the same reason we log-transformed nothing extra here, unlike a raw-power pipeline would need to). With ~32,000 channel x frequency points, checking each one individually is neither possible nor useful; instead we check a handful of representative points.

docs.title: 1.5 Covariate strategy¶
docs.text: Age and CRIq are covariates, as in Case Study 1. We use partial correlation: correlate log-power with MoCA after removing the linear effect of age and CRIq from both variables. This is simpler to explain than a two-step residualisation and gives the same result.

docs.title: 2.2 Baseline — a Case-Study-1-style model¶
docs.text: Before analysing the whole spectrum, we fit the kind of model Case Study 1 would use: a single, a-priori ERP feature (P300 amplitude) as a predictor of MoCA. This is deliberately naive here — P300 and resting- state PSD are conceptually different recordings (task-based vs. resting), so this model cannot detect the whole-scalp resting-state association we are looking for. It exists only to make the contrast concrete: a model that commits in advance to one feature can only find an association if it happens to live there.

docs.title: 2.3 Mass-univariate partial correlation¶
docs.text: We now use the real, full-resolution spectrum. At every channel x frequency point, we compute the partial correlation between log-power and MoCA, controlling for age and CRIq, and convert it to a t-statistic. This produces one map of 204 x 159 test statistics.

docs.title: 2.4 Cluster-based permutation test¶
docs.text:
The idea, in plain terms: instead of correcting each point in isolation, we group neighbouring suprathreshold points into clusters (a point is a neighbour of another if they are adjacent channels at the same frequency, or the same channel at adjacent frequency bins), sum the t-values within each cluster, and ask: if MoCA were randomly shuffled across participants (so any true association is destroyed), how often would a cluster this large arise purely by chance? We estimate that by actually shuffling MoCA thousands of times and recomputing the largest cluster each time — this is the permutation null distribution. A cluster's p-value is simply the fraction of shuffles that produced a cluster at least as extreme as the one we observed.

Spatial adjacency comes from the real 3D positions of the EGI-256 montage (via mne.channels.find_ch_adjacency); spectral adjacency links consecutive frequency bins (Maris & Oostenveld, 2007).

We run two, pre-planned analyses:

  • Primary — the whole spectrum (1–40 Hz), every channel, no a priori restriction. This is the test the paper's framing is built around: it can find an effect anywhere, at the cost of a large multiple- comparisons penalty.
  • Secondary / confirmatory — restricted a priori to the region the clinical literature actually predicts (right hemisphere, delta/theta, 1–8 Hz). Restricting the search space before looking at the data is standard practice when there is a specific hypothesis, and it recovers power the whole-spectrum test gives up. We report both, rather than only the one that "worked", precisely to avoid the circular reasoning Case Study 1 warned about (Section 2.3 there): the secondary result is only informative because it was planned, not because we went looking for whichever restriction happened to be significant.

docs.title: 2.5 Where is the effect? (topography of the significant cluster)¶
docs.text: For the significant cluster from the secondary analysis, we plot a topographic map of the (partial-correlation) r-values, averaged over the cluster's frequency range, with the cluster's channels highlighted.

docs.title: 2.6 Illustrative check: PSD by MoCA level¶
docs.text: Purely for illustration (not a separate statistical test), we split participants by a median MoCA split and plot the average spectrum at the cluster's channels for each group.

docs.title: 2.7 Exploratory: which canonical band drives the effect?¶
docs.text:
The secondary analysis above pools delta and theta (1–8 Hz) into a single test. It is natural to ask whether the effect is really carried by both, or mainly by one of them — and whether it is genuinely absent in alpha/beta/gamma, as the clinical hypothesis would predict.

This is an exploratory, supplementary analysis, not a substitute for the pre-registered primary/secondary tests above. We repeat the same cluster-permutation procedure (same right-hemisphere ROI, same threshold) separately for each of the five canonical bands. Because this means testing five hypotheses instead of one, we apply a Bonferroni correction across bands (multiply each band's p-value by 5, capped at 1) — exactly the kind of correction Case Study 1 discussed for multiple outcomes, applied here to multiple frequency bands instead.

docs.title: 3. Export¶
docs.text: Same philosophy as Case Study 1: figures as PNG, tables as both CSV and a single Excel workbook.

docs.title: 4. Strengths and limitations of this approach (Section 4.2.3)¶
docs.text:
Strengths:

  • No a priori commitment to a specific band or region — able to recover a distributed, low-frequency, right-hemisphere pattern that no single ERP feature (Case Study 1) would capture (Section 2.2 above)
  • Respects the real spatial and spectral dependency structure of the signal, unlike testing every point independently

Limitations:

  • Computationally heavier than the GLM-based approach of Case Study 1
  • Statistically demanding: with around forty participants, cluster-based permutation is relatively underpowered, so only fairly marked associations are likely to survive — the whole-spectrum (primary) test in Section 2.4 illustrates this directly
  • A significant secondary result depends on having pre-registered the restricted region before looking at the data; restricting only after seeing what "worked" would be the same circular reasoning Case Study 1 warned against, just at the level of search space instead of predictor selection

For a full discussion, see Section 4.2 of the companion paper, and Section 5.1 on general caveats (multiple comparisons, and not equating analytical complexity with validity).

read_npy <- function(path) {
  # Minimal reader for the subset of the .npy format we actually need:
  # version 1.0/2.0 header, C-order (row-major), float32/float64 data.
  con <- file(path, "rb")
  on.exit(close(con))
  magic <- readBin(con, "raw", n = 6)
  stopifnot(rawToChar(magic[2:6]) == "NUMPY")
  major <- readBin(con, "integer", n = 1, size = 1, signed = FALSE)
  readBin(con, "integer", n = 1, size = 1, signed = FALSE)  # minor version, unused
  header_len <- if (major == 1) {
    readBin(con, "integer", n = 1, size = 2, signed = FALSE, endian = "little")
  } else {
    readBin(con, "integer", n = 1, size = 4, endian = "little")
  }
  header <- rawToChar(readBin(con, "raw", n = header_len))
  stopifnot(!grepl("'fortran_order':\\s*True", header))  # we only handle C order

  shape_str <- regmatches(header, regexpr("(?<=\'shape\':\\s\\()[^)]*", header, perl = TRUE))
  shape <- as.integer(trimws(strsplit(shape_str, ",")[[1]]))
  shape <- shape[!is.na(shape)]
  descr <- regmatches(header, regexpr("(?<=\'descr\':\\s\')[^\']+", header, perl = TRUE))
  size <- if (grepl("f8", descr)) 8 else 4

  vals <- readBin(con, "double", n = prod(shape), size = size, endian = "little")
  if (length(shape) == 1) return(vals)
  # row-major data into a column-major R array: fill with reversed
  # dims, then transpose the axis order back
  aperm(array(vals, dim = rev(shape)), rev(seq_along(shape)))
}

partial_corr_tmap <- function(log_power, y, age, criq, n_ch_, n_freq_) {
  # partial-correlation t-map of log_power vs y, controlling age & criq.
  # Returns a flat vector, index = (ch-1)*n_freq_ + freq (1-indexed),
  # i.e. channel-major, matching combine_adjacency() below.
  n <- length(y)
  Z <- cbind(1, age, criq)
  Z_pinv <- ginv(Z)
  resid_y <- y - Z %*% (Z_pinv %*% y)
  Y <- matrix(aperm(log_power, c(1, 3, 2)), nrow = n)
  resid_power <- Y - Z %*% (Z_pinv %*% Y)
  num <- as.vector(t(resid_y) %*% resid_power)
  den <- sqrt(sum(resid_y^2)) * sqrt(colSums(resid_power^2))
  r <- pmax(pmin(num / den, 0.999999), -0.999999)
  df <- n - 4   # n - intercept - age - criq - y
  r * sqrt(df / (1 - r^2))
}

find_clusters <- function(t_flat, t_thresh, adjacency) {
  clusters <- list()
  for (sign in c(1, -1)) {
    supra <- which((t_flat * sign) > t_thresh)
    if (length(supra) == 0) next
    # build the suprathreshold subgraph straight from the sparse
    # adjacency's own (i, j) triplets, without ever densifying it
    sub_adj <- as(adjacency[supra, supra], "TsparseMatrix")
    el <- cbind(sub_adj@i + 1L, sub_adj@j + 1L)
    el <- el[el[, 1] < el[, 2], , drop = FALSE]
    g <- make_empty_graph(n = length(supra), directed = FALSE)
    if (nrow(el) > 0) g <- add_edges(g, as.vector(t(el)))
    comp <- components(g)
    for (k in seq_len(comp$no)) {
      members <- supra[comp$membership == k]
      clusters[[length(clusters) + 1]] <- list(members = members, mass = sum(t_flat[members]))
    }
  }
  clusters
}

cluster_permutation_test <- function(log_power, y, age, criq, adjacency, n_ch_, n_freq_,
                                      t_thresh = 2.028, n_perm = 2000, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  t_obs <- partial_corr_tmap(log_power, y, age, criq, n_ch_, n_freq_)
  obs_clusters <- find_clusters(t_obs, t_thresh, adjacency)
  obs_clusters <- obs_clusters[order(-abs(sapply(obs_clusters, function(c) c$mass)))]
  n <- length(y)
  null_max <- numeric(n_perm)
  for (i in seq_len(n_perm)) {
    shuffled <- sample(n)
    t_perm <- partial_corr_tmap(log_power, y[shuffled], age, criq, n_ch_, n_freq_)
    cl <- find_clusters(t_perm, t_thresh, adjacency)
    null_max[i] <- if (length(cl) == 0) 0 else max(abs(sapply(cl, function(c) c$mass)))
  }
  results <- list()
  top <- obs_clusters[seq_len(min(5, length(obs_clusters)))]
  for (c in top) {
    p <- mean(null_max >= abs(c$mass))
    results[[length(results) + 1]] <- list(members = c$members, mass = c$mass, p_cluster = p)
  }
  list(clusters = results, t_obs = flat_to_map(t_obs, n_ch_, n_freq_))
}

# Cartesian-product adjacency over the (channel x freq) grid: two points
# are neighbours iff (same freq, adjacent channels) or (same channel,
# adjacent freq bins) - the R equivalent of mne.stats.combine_adjacency().
combine_adjacency <- function(spatial_adj, n_freq_) {
  nch_ <- nrow(spatial_adj)
  kronecker(spatial_adj, Diagonal(n_freq_)) + kronecker(Diagonal(nch_), freq_chain_adjacency(n_freq_))
}

What do we see in the plots?

Each panel is one canonical band, coloured by the same t-value scale; a panel's channels would be marked if that band's cluster survived correction for having tested five bands. First, it is a direct, concrete illustration of why multiple-comparison correction matters: taken on its own, theta's raw p-value would look like a finding — it only stops looking like one once we account for having tested five bands instead of pre-committing to one.
